title: Telling, asking, and forbidding
goal: Ask for things without sounding bossy — a skill that matters more in Javanese than in almost any language you may know, because a bare command sounds far harsher here than it does in English.
bekal: forming commands with the suffixes *-a*, *-en*, and *-na*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Nyuwun tulung marang Pak Broto
dialogs.intro: The water in the bathroom has stopped. Dian goes to see Pak Broto — a request to an older person, so it is all in krama. Then Rini comes along and the tone of the conversation changes at once.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Nuwun sèwu, Pak. Kula badhé nyuwun tulung.
lines.id: Excuse me, sir. I'd like to ask for your help.
lines.literal: beg thousand, sir. I will beg help.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Toya ing jedhing mboten medal wiwit wau énjing.
lines.id: The water in the bathroom hasn't come out since this morning.
lines.literal: water in bathroom not come-out since earlier morning.

lines.speaker: Pak Broto:
lines.text: O, nggih. Mangké kula priksani. Sekedhap nggih.
lines.id: Oh, I see. I'll check it later. Just a moment.
lines.literal: oh, yes. later I check. moment yes.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: Thank you so much, sir. Sorry for the trouble.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Yan, tulung jupukna émbèr ing ngisor, ya!
lines.id: Yan, please get me the bucket downstairs!
lines.literal: Yan, please take-for-me bucket at below, yes!

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Iya. Aja lali, sing gedhé, dudu sing cilik.
lines.id: Yes. Don't forget, the big one, not the small one.
lines.literal: yes. don't forget, which big, not which small.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Iya, sedhéla. Coba deloken, banyuné wis mili durung?
lines.id: OK, just a sec. Have a look, is the water running yet?
lines.literal: yes, moment. try look-at-it, water-the already flow not-yet?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Durung. Ayo, ngentèni waé ing ngarep.
lines.id: Not yet. Come on, let's just wait out front.
lines.literal: not-yet. come-on, wait just at front.

notes: **Nyuwun tulung** (krama) / **njaluk tulung** (ngoko) is the safest way to open a request. It tells the listener that what follows is a request, not an order — and that is half the job done.

**Ngrepoti** means "to cause trouble", said after someone agrees to help. It isn't a real apology; it is part of good manners, like "sorry to trouble you" in English. Leaving it out makes your request feel flat.

**Sampun kuwatir** — here *sampun* means "don't", not "already". This is the word that confuses beginners most. How to tell them apart: *sampun* + a verb that **hasn't happened** = don't; *sampun* + something that **has** happened = already. The tone of voice usually differs too.
**Mboten** is another form of *boten* (not), equally correct and equally common. The same goes for *mangga* / *monggo* and *inggih* / *nggih*: spoken Javanese keeps many pairs like these.
**Jupukna** = *jupuk* + the suffix *-na*, meaning "get it (for me)". Compare *jupuken*, "take it (that thing)". One letter separates two different commands.

**Deloken** = *deleng* + *-en*, "look at it". Notice that the last vowel of the root changes when the suffix is attached — *deleng* → *deloken*. Changes like this are regular but numerous; at A1, just memorize the common forms as they are.
**Mili** means "to flow". It comes up in many everyday contexts: water, traffic, money.

grammars.title: Three command forms, and how they differ
body: Javanese distinguishes **who is told to act** from **what the action is done to**, and the difference is marked with suffixes. English doesn't do this, so this part is genuinely new — but there are only three forms.

head: Form
Meaning
Example
Translation
rows: command **for the benefit** of the speaker

after: **The difference between *-en* and *-na* is subtle but real**: *tukokna* = buy it (for me); *tukunen* = buy it (that item). When in doubt, use *tulung* + the root: *tulung tuku* is understood by everyone and is never wrong.

**A command with no suffix sounds harsh.** *Mangan!* to an adult feels like snapping at them. The natural thing is to add a softener: *mangana* (with *-a*), or *mangan ya* (with *ya* at the end), or *ayo mangan* (as an invitation).

**In krama, commands are almost always wrapped in the passive**: *mangga dipun-dhahar* (please, it is to be eaten), *mangga dipun-lenggahi* (please, it is to be sat on). Ordering a respected person directly — *panjenengan dhahar!* — sounds wrong, even though the words are krama.

sections.title: Softening: five words that change the tone

blocks.text: In Javanese, **how you ask matters more than what you ask for**. These five words are the main tools, and they can all be used together.

head: Word
Position
Function
Example
rows: softens it into an invitation to try

blocks.text: Compare these three sentences, all asking for the same thing:

items: *Jupuk banyu!* — Get water! Sounds like an order to a small child or a subordinate.
*Jupukna banyu, ya.* — Get me some water, OK? Normal between friends.
*Nuwun sèwu, nyuwun tulung mendhetaken toya, nggih.* — Excuse me, could you please get me some water? Fully polite, for someone you respect.

blocks.title: Why this matters more in Javanese
items: English allows a fairly neutral direct request ("grab some water"). Javanese has no equally neutral tone: a bare command falls into ngoko, and ngoko to the wrong person reads as condescending.

That is why Javanese speakers often ask **without any command verb at all** — they just state the situation and let the listener draw the conclusion: *toya-nipun mboten medal, Pak* (the water isn't coming out, sir). That is already a complete request, and it is exactly what Dian does in the dialogue.
This technique works everywhere and is never rude. If you remember only one thing from this unit, remember that **naming the problem is enough**.

blocks.text: **Aja** and **sampun** are only for forbidding actions. To negate a statement you still use *ora* / *boten*, and to negate a noun you use *dudu* / *sanès*. Three words for three jobs — compare English "don't", "not", and "not a".

exercises.prompt: Change these verbs into gentle commands with the suffix **-a**.
Choose *-en* (command about a thing) or *-na* (get it for me).
items: Buku kuwi wac____ dhisik. (read the book)
Tulung jupuk____ banyu. (get some water for me)
Tuko____ gedhang loro. (buy me two bananas)

exercises.prompt: Turn these rude commands into polite requests in krama.
**Review of Unit 10.** Cover Unit 10, then write these sentences in Javanese.
items: The one that isn't spicy, please. (ngoko)
How much is it all together? (krama)

answers: Mangga, nyuwun tulung mendhetaken toya. — Mangga dipun-dhahar. — Mangga lenggah. — Sampun késah rumiyin, nggih. — Nyuwun tulung ngentosi sekedhap.
Sega goréng wonten? — Sing ora pedhes, ya. — Dibungkus waé. — Sedaya pinten? — Éca sanget.
